opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually something every team working on models should try at least once, even if you don't plan to ship it as a product. When you build or improve an agent framework yourself, you start to see very concretely where the model breaks. On benchmarks, a model can look very strong, but once you put it inside a real loop of planning, calling tools, reading results, and correcting itself, small weaknesses compound. A slightly unstable instruction-following ability, or a tendency to lose track of context after many steps, suddenly becomes the main bottleneck.

So for me, the framework isn't really the goal. It's more like an instrument. It tells you what the model needs to learn. If you find yourself writing a lot of hand-crafted rules, retries, or prompt tricks to patch over failures, that's usually a signal that the capability should be pushed back into the model through better data or training, rather than piling more engineering on top.

At the same time, I'd be careful not to over-invest in very complex scaffolding. Model capabilities are improving quickly, and a lot of clever framework design from six months ago becomes unnecessary once the base model gets better at long-horizon reasoning and tool use. The more durable parts tend to be the simple ones: a clean environment, good tool interfaces, reliable feedback signals, and a way to evaluate end-to-end task success.

So my view is: build it yourself, keep it simple, and use it mainly to understand and improve the model. The real progress usually comes from closing that loop between what the agent struggles with and what you train the model on next.

r001.rationale: The response says a framework helps reveal model weaknesses, but does not judge improvements insufficient when others cannot perceive its intelligence.

r002.rationale: The response recommends building a framework and keeping it simple, but does not say that one person working on it would lead to slow improvement.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: Honestly, I think the agent framework itself is the easy part. If you look at what's out there today, the frameworks are mostly thin wrappers: a loop that calls the model, parses a tool call, executes it, feeds the result back. Anyone can write that in a few hundred lines. So when people ask me whether it's worth building your own, my answer is that the framework is not where the value sits. The value sits in the model and in how well the model and the framework fit each other.

When I was doing this myself, what I found was that most of the "improvements" people make to frameworks are actually compensating for weaknesses in the model. You add a planner module because the model doesn't plan well. You add a reflection step because the model doesn't notice its own mistakes. You add memory retrieval because the context window is too small or the model doesn't use long context well. Every one of those pieces is a patch. And the problem with patches is that when the model gets better, the patch becomes dead weight, or worse, it actively gets in the way. I've seen cases where a heavily engineered scaffold performs worse with a stronger model than a simple loop does, because the scaffold was tuned around the old model's failure modes.

So my view is that if you're serious, you should treat the framework and the model as one system. You don't improve the framework in isolation. You look at where the agent fails, and then you ask: is this a framework problem or a model problem? Usually it's a model problem. And then the right move is to go fix it at the training level, whether that's data, whether that's RL, whether that's how you expose tools during training. The framework should get simpler over time, not more complex. That's actually my test for whether a team is on the right track. If their agent code keeps growing, they're probably fighting the model. If it's shrinking, the model is doing more of the work.

That said, there's one thing I would spend real effort on, and that's the environment and the evaluation. Building good environments where the agent can act, fail, and get feedback is genuinely hard, and it's where I think a small team can still make a difference. The framework is commodity. The environments and the data that come out of them are not.

r001.rationale: The response says framework improvements often patch model weaknesses, but does not say they are insufficient when others cannot perceive the framework’s intelligence.

r002.rationale: The response does not claim that improvement would be slow if only one person worked on the framework.

astra-6.text:
I’d start with a concrete task and look at where the agent struggles. Does it misunderstand the goal, choose the wrong tool, lose track of context, or fail to recognize a mistake? Those problems need different solutions, so I wouldn’t begin by redesigning the whole framework.

Working on your own, you need a tight feedback loop: inspect a failure, make a small change, and check whether it helps across several tasks. It’s easy to add complexity that improves one example but makes the system less reliable overall. For me, improving a framework means making its behavior easier to understand and its results more dependable—not simply giving it more features.

r001.rationale: The response discusses making behavior understandable and results dependable, but does not say individual improvements are insufficient unless other people can perceive the framework’s intelligence.

r002.rationale: It describes how one person can improve the framework, but does not suggest that progress would be slow with only one person working on it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first step is to clarify what you want the agent to do better. Is it failing to understand the task, choosing the wrong tools, or losing track of information over a long interaction? Those are different problems, and changing the framework won’t necessarily solve all of them.

If I were working on it on my own, I’d start with a small set of concrete tasks, look closely at the failures, and improve one component at a time. Then I’d check whether the change helps across those tasks. The important thing is to build a reliable feedback loop: observe, make a change, and verify it. Otherwise, it’s easy to add complexity without making the agent more useful.

r001.rationale: The response discusses identifying failures and checking whether changes help, but it does not say improvements are insufficient unless other people can perceive the framework’s intelligence.

r002.rationale: It describes how one person could improve the framework, but does not suggest that solo work would make improvement slow.
